title: Best Paymentology Alternatives for African Fintechs
summary: Compare the top Paymentology alternatives for African fintechs. Evaluate issuer-processors, card APIs, float management, launch speed, and Miden's unified infrastructure.
body_markdown:
Choosing a card-issuing provider in Africa goes beyond Visa and Mastercard connectivity. You also need to navigate issuing markets, sponsorship, settlement currencies, and float management.


​While Paymentology is an established issuer-processor strong with traditional banks, fintechs needing local accounts, collections, and multi-currency liquidity often outgrow pure-play processors.


​This guide compares six Paymentology alternatives, including Miden, Marqeta, Galileo, Thredd, Pismo, and Stripe Issuing, breaking down their architecture, coverage, and capabilities to help you choose the right infrastructure for your business.


## Paymentology: Core Capabilities and Scaling Constraints for African Fintechs


Formed in 2021 by merging Paymentology UK with South Africa’s Tutuka (est. 1998), Paymentology processes cards for over 400 clients across 65+ countries, including Standard Bank and Access Bank.


Its platform covers direct Visa and Mastercard connectivity, multi-cloud processing, 3D Secure, and a Decision Engine to build and back-test real-time authorization rules. It also runs managed programs and matches fintechs with BIN sponsors, letting teams avoid building proprietary processing rails.


Scaling on the platform involves key operational hurdles for African teams:


- **Sponsorship dependencies:** Partnering with a matched BIN sponsor requires a separate contract, adding distinct underwriting requirements, compliance checks, and pricing.
- **Go-to-market speed:** The managed program route can deliver cards in eight weeks. Custom setups assembled with separate sponsor and clearing partners face compounding approval cycles and longer timelines.
- **Float and settlement:** Cross-currency programs (USD and local African currencies) demand explicit terms on where collateral funds sit, FX conversion execution, and daily settlement speed.


These demands suit established banks and mature fintechs equipped with existing licenses and treasury operations. Leaner startups needing turnkey infrastructure may prefer an all-in-one provider to avoid juggling multiple counterparty relationships.


## Key Takeaways


- None of Marqeta, Galileo, Thredd, Pismo or Stripe Issuing publishes domestic issuing in African markets that we could confirm.
- Time to market depends less on the processor than on how many third parties sit around it.
- Miden suits fintechs and enterprises that want cards, NGN and USD accounts, treasury and payouts on one ledger in the markets it serves.

## 1. Miden


**Best for:** African fintechs, platforms and enterprises that want fast-to-deploy card issuing unified with multi-currency accounts, automated float liquidity and local settlement.


Miden is a YC-backed card issuer, processor and[banking software](https://www.miden.co/core-banking) company located in Lagos. It sits between a pure processor and a turnkey card program. You get virtual and physical card issuing alongside multi-currency virtual accounts and automated payouts, all running on a single ledger.


That means the cards you issue draw on the same balances that handle your collections and vendor settlements, and Miden's model is that sponsorship and local settlement sit inside the platform instead of being separate contracts for you to negotiate.


### Key Technical Capabilities


- **Full-Stack Architecture:** Cards are built on Miden's[Banking Stack](https://www.miden.co/banking-stack) ,[Global Treasury](https://www.miden.co/global-treasury) and[Accruals and Disbursements](https://www.miden.co/accruals-disbursements) products, so issuing, accounts and payouts share one API.
- **Dynamic Authorization and Spend Controls:** In Miden-managed mode, balance checks, merchant category restrictions, velocity limits and fraud checks run against rules you set in the dashboard. In customer-managed mode, Miden sends your service an encrypted, HMAC-signed callback and you answer, approve or decline within 400 milliseconds. Channel rules cover ATM, web and POS.
- **Unified Float Management:** Cards draw on a pooled, multi-currency treasury account in NGN and USD, so you do not preload each card.
- **Local and Regional Rails:** NGN and USD virtual accounts for collections, NIP transfers, and M-Pesa payouts run on the same ledger as your cards.
- **Developer and Wallet Support:** A REST API, a dashboard, and tap-to-pay for Apple Pay, Google Pay and Samsung Pay (added in March 2026), with Miden's support team handling onboarding.


### Pricing


Miden quotes per programme, based on volumes, card types and currency corridors. It is not publicly listed.


### Considerations


Miden onboards verified businesses, so KYB and compliance vetting are required, and it is not designed for hobby projects or low-volume tests. Its issuing footprint covers Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania and Sierra Leone, so confirm coverage if you need cards elsewhere.


### Verdict


For African fintechs that would otherwise assemble sponsorship, settlement, float and payouts from separate vendors, Miden is the most complete route on this list, and the one built around the rails and currencies you actually settle in.


## 2. Marqeta


**Best for:** High-volume global platforms and enterprise marketplaces that need programmable transaction routing and already operate in Marqeta's certified licensing corridors.


Marqeta (NASDAQ: MQ) pioneered modern open-API issuer processing and powers large-scale programs for global platforms such as DoorDash, Klarna, and Uber. Operating as a certified processor across more than 40 countries, the platform decouples business authorization logic from core payment rails, giving enterprise engineering teams granular programmatic control over card behavior.


**Key Technical Capabilities**


- **Just-in-Time (JIT) Funding:** Zero-balance card architecture that holds authorizations open while Marqeta forwards transaction metadata to your webhook endpoint. Your application approves or declines the transaction in real time and transfers the exact funds required on demand.
- **Granular Transaction Controls:** Real-time velocity rules, dynamic MCC whitelisting/blacklisting, geolocation parameters, and balance limits configurable via dashboard or API.
- **Extensive API Surface:** Over 300 RESTful endpoints handling card provisioning, programmatic cardholder management, ledger tracking, and automated 3D Secure workflows.
- **Tokenization & Wallet Provisioning:** Standalone and integrated network tokenization supporting Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Samsung Pay with push-provisioning SDKs.


### Pricing


Custom enterprise pricing. Contracts are negotiated around monthly API call minimums, interchange sharing agreements, and per-authorization fees.


### Considerations


Marqeta’s certified domestic issuing remains focused across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific, with no direct African domestic clearing or settlement rails. An African fintech using Marqeta must assemble external BIN sponsorship, local currency liquidity, and banking partners independently.


### Verdict


An exceptional processing engine for multinational enterprises operating in supported Western and APAC corridors, but requiring substantial multi-vendor assembly for African operations.


## 3. Galileo


**Best for:** Fintechs, digital banks, and retail brands in North America and Latin America seeking an established core banking ledger paired with issuer processing.


A subsidiary of SoFi Technologies, Galileo is one of North America’s foundational fintech processing engines, powering platforms such as Chime and Robinhood. Following its acquisition and integration of Technisys, Galileo pairs cloud-native issuer processing with Cyberbank core banking infrastructure, allowing institutions to run deposit accounts, lending programs, and card processing within a single operational environment.


### Key Technical Capabilities


- **Galileo Processing API:** Mature REST APIs supporting debit, credit, prepaid, and virtual card issuance with real-time authorization callbacks and custom decision routing.
- **Integrated Core Banking (Technisys):** Cloud-native multi-product engine supporting checking, savings, credit lines, and real-time ledger accounting without external core software.
- **Direct Switch Certifications:** Local Mastercard domestic switch certification in Mexico, supporting localized clearing, routing, and interchange optimization across Latin America.
- **Fraud & Risk Intelligence:** Galileo Analytics and Risk Engine provide automated fraud scoring, transaction behavioral analysis, and dispute resolution management.


### Pricing


Custom volume-based pricing determined by account volume, transaction activity, and integrated core banking modules.


### Considerations


Galileo has no domestic presence or clearing integrations across African payment networks. It is primarily relevant to African organizations launching retail programs directly within the US or Latin American markets.


### Verdict


A formidable combined processor and core banking engine for the Americas, though structurally disconnected from African domestic banking rails and settlement networks.


## 4. Thredd


**Best for:** European and Asia-Pacific fintechs and digital banks seeking an AI-first issuer processor with proven multi-currency scale and native automated risk controls.


Operating across 44 countries with direct scheme certifications, Thredd (formerly Global Processing Services / GPS) has evolved from an early backer of high-growth European fintechs, including Revolut, Starling Bank, and Curve, into an AI-first issuer processing platform.


Beyond high-availability authorization, the platform places heavy emphasis on integrated machine learning across its transaction and risk infrastructure, helping issuers cut operational overhead without bolting on disjointed third-party engines.


### Key Technical Capabilities


- **AI & Adaptive Risk Management:** Rather than relying solely on static rules, Thredd integrates adaptive behavioural analytics and machine learning (partnered with Featurespace). It models customer transaction patterns in real time to catch emerging fraud vectors and authorised push payment (APP) scams while slashing false-positive declines.
- **External Host Interface (EHI):** Real-time transaction streaming into client systems, supporting both full host authorization (client-approved logic) and cooperative processing modes.
- **Flexible Program Configurations:** Multi-currency processing across debit, credit, prepaid, and virtual cards, alongside multi-wallet architectures designed for international spend.
- **Partner-Led BIN Sponsorship:** Structured integration paths with regulated sponsor banks such as Cross River Bank (US) and FinXP (Europe) to manage compliance and scheme licensing.


### Pricing


Negotiated enterprise contracts calculated on monthly active card volumes, authorization throughput, risk tiering, and level of dedicated technical account support.


### Considerations


While Thredd supplies the core processing and native ML intelligence, it functions on an unbundled model, relying on external partner banks for licensing, settlement accounts, and daily treasury float management. Crucially for African operators, Thredd lacks domestic African BIN partners, local currency clearing rails, and native mobile money integrations.


### Verdict


A battle-tested, AI-driven processor for global and European digital banking initiatives that still leaves African fintechs with the burden of independently sourcing local banking and settlement partners.


## 5. Pismo (Visa)


**Best for:** Mid-to-large tier financial institutions, legacy banks, and tier-one enterprises modernizing their core banking infrastructure and card issuing on a single cloud platform.


Founded in Brazil and acquired by Visa for $1 billion, Pismo provides an integrated, cloud-native core banking and issuer processing platform built on microservices. Designed to replace aging legacy bank mainframes, Pismo enables traditional banks and large fintechs to spin up digital accounts, manage lending programs, and issue commercial or consumer cards through one cloud infrastructure layer.


### Key Technical Capabilities


- **Unified Cloud Core & Processing:** Microservice architecture running on AWS and Google Cloud that combines checking/savings ledgers, credit engines, and card switching into a single backend.
- **Comprehensive Card Issuance:** API-driven provisioning for debit, credit, prepaid, and corporate commercial card structures with multi-currency balance capabilities.
- **Native Fast Payment Rails:** Built-in connectivity for real-time payment architectures, including instant clearing integrations like Pix in Brazil.
- **Event-Driven Webhook Streaming:** Real-time data streaming for balance updates, authorization routing, transaction clearance, and ledger reconciliation.


### Pricing


Enterprise-grade pricing structured for financial institutions, typically involving upfront implementation costs, software licensing, and processing volume tiers.


### Considerations


Pismo is engineered primarily as a full-scale core replacement or major institutional build, carrying high implementation overhead that is ill-suited for agile startups simply seeking fast virtual card deployment. Local domestic issuing across African corridors is not confirmed.


### Verdict


An enterprise-grade cloud banking and processing powerhouse for major institutions overhauling core systems, but over-engineered for fintechs looking to launch card programs quickly.


## 6. Stripe Issuing


**Best for:** Existing Stripe merchants, SaaS platforms, and internet businesses in supported regions looking to launch expense or commercial cards with minimal development time.


Stripe Issuing brings card creation directly into the broader Stripe payments architecture. Built as an embedded product rather than an enterprise processing engine, it allows platforms already processing payments with Stripe to direct incoming transaction revenues straight into spendable virtual and physical commercial cards, eliminating the need to source external banking sponsors or build custom ledgers.


### Key Technical Capabilities


- **Direct Balance Funding:** Authorizations draw directly from your platform's existing Stripe balance, funding cards instantly without external bank wires or manual account preloading.
- **Real-Time Webhook Authorizations:** Custom authorization webhooks allow your system to approve or decline transaction requests within a two-second window based on platform-level rules.
- **Stripe Issuing Elements:** Secure, pre-built client-side UI components that display sensitive card details (PAN, CVV) directly in your web or mobile app, minimizing PCI DSS compliance scope.
- **Automated Spend Restrictions:** Dashboard-driven or API-configured restrictions covering transaction amount limits, currency controls, allowed merchant categories, and velocity rules.


### Pricing


Transparent, pay-as-you-go pricing: $0.10 per virtual card and $3.50 per standard physical card in the US, plus standard domestic transaction processing and interchange split terms. Custom pricing is available for high-volume programs.


### Considerations


Local domestic card issuing is restricted to roughly 22 markets across North America, the UK, and Europe. Stripe does not support local domestic card issuing, local settlement accounts, or regional rails (such as NIP or M-Pesa) across Africa.


### Verdict


The cleanest and quickest embedded issuing tool for startups operating in Stripe-supported Western markets, but unable to service domestic African issuing or settlement needs.


## What Should You Look for in a Card-Issuing Provider in Africa?


Choosing a card-issuing provider requires looking beyond the processing API. The provider's architecture, settlement arrangements, authorization controls and commercial terms will all affect how your programme operates as transaction volumes grow.


### 1. Full-Stack or Component-Based Architecture


A processor handles card transactions, but it may not provide the issuing sponsor, settlement accounts, KYB onboarding or funding infrastructure. Find out which services come with the platform and which require separate providers.


### 2. Settlement Predictability and Multi-Currency Liquidity


For programmes involving NGN, USD or other currencies, examine how funds move between collection, card authorization and settlement. Ask where balances are held, who handles conversion, which exchange rates apply and when settled funds become available.


### 3. Authorization Webhooks and Latency


Real-time authorization allows a card programme to apply its own balance checks, spending rules and risk decisions when a transaction arrives. However, customer-managed authorization depends on your service responding within the provider's permitted time window.


Ask how long you have to approve or decline a transaction, what happens when your endpoint times out, and whether the provider supports managed authorization rules as an alternative. Test response times under realistic transaction loads before launch.


### 4. Card Data and PCI DSS Scope


How a provider exposes card details affects the security requirements placed on your own systems. Compare how each provider handles card data, encryption, tokenization and digital wallet provisioning. Ask for a clear explanation of the PCI DSS obligations that will apply to your specific integration.


### 5. Scalable Commercial Terms


A card programme's costs extend beyond the price of issuing a physical or virtual card. Request a breakdown of setup fees, monthly minimums, authorization charges, transaction fees, settlement costs and foreign exchange margins.

## Frequently Asked Questions


**1. What are the best alternatives to Paymentology for African fintechs?**


**Miden** is the top choice if you want unified card issuing combined with NGN and USD accounts, treasury, and payouts across supported African markets. Alternatives like Marqeta, Galileo, Thredd, and Stripe Issuing cater to other regions, while Pismo targets institutions merging core banking with processing.


**2. What is the difference between an issuer-processor and a full-stack card issuing platform?**


An issuer-processor handles authorization, scheme connectivity and transaction switching. A full-stack platform like Miden adds the surrounding pieces, such as accounts, funding, settlement and onboarding, so you manage fewer vendors.


**3. Why do African fintechs outgrow or avoid pure issuer-processors?**


Traditional setups force you to juggle multiple vendors for BIN sponsorship, settlement accounts, currency liquidity, and payouts. Fintechs choose Miden to eliminate this operational overhead and manage everything through a single integrated platform.


**4. Does Miden support both local African and international currencies?**


**Yes.** Miden supports NGN and USD virtual accounts, issues virtual and physical cards in both, and operates in key markets including Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, and Sierra Leone.


**5. How long does it take to launch a card programme with Miden?**


​Timelines vary based on your KYB verification, custom requirements, and integration scope. Unlike generic vendor claims, Miden provides a transparent, tailored implementation plan during your onboarding session.
